title: Diarrhea After Drinking: Why It Happens and How to Stop It
excerpt: Why alcohol gives you diarrhea the next morning, why liquor can be worse, how long it lasts, what helps, and the warning signs that mean you should see a doctor.

author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** diarrhea after drinking is common, usually harmless, and usually gone within a day. Alcohol speeds up the movement of your gut, makes your intestines worse at pulling water back into your body, and irritates the lining of your stomach and bowel. Add in sugary mixers, carbonation, greasy late-night food, and a morning coffee, and loose stools the next day are almost predictable. Most of the time the fix is boring: fluids with some salt and sugar, bland food, rest, and time.

**The quick rules:** Sip fluids steadily (water plus an oral rehydration drink or broth), eat small bland meals, skip more alcohol and go easy on coffee until things settle, and give it 24 to 48 hours. Diarrhea that comes with blood, black stools, a fever, severe belly pain, or signs of dehydration is not a normal hangover symptom and needs a doctor.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Get medical help if** you see blood in your stool or your stool is black and tarry; the diarrhea lasts more than 2 days; you have a fever above 102°F (39°C); you have severe or constant belly pain, especially pain in the upper abdomen that spreads to your back; you are vomiting and can't keep fluids down; or you have signs of dehydration such as dizziness when you stand, a racing heart, very dark urine, or barely urinating. **If you drink heavily most days** and get diarrhea along with shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you cut back, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor rather than riding it out. In an emergency, call 911.

## Why Alcohol Gives You Diarrhea: The Gut Mechanics in Plain Words

Your digestive tract does two jobs that matter here. It moves food along with rhythmic muscle contractions (called motility), and it absorbs water and salts back into your body as food passes through. Normal, formed stool is the result of those two jobs being in balance: things move at a steady pace, and enough water gets pulled out along the way. Diarrhea happens when stool moves too fast, when too little water gets absorbed, when extra water gets drawn into the gut, or some mix of all three. Alcohol can push on every one of those.

### 1. Alcohol speeds up the small intestine

Research on gut motility has found that alcohol changes the pattern of muscle contractions in the intestines. In the stomach, higher-strength drinks tend to slow emptying, which is part of why you can feel bloated and queasy. Further down, in the small intestine, alcohol tends to speed things up. When food and fluid rush through faster than normal, your gut has less time to absorb water and nutrients, so more liquid arrives in the colon than it can handle.

### 2. Alcohol makes your gut worse at absorbing water and salt

The lining of your small intestine is covered in tiny cells that pull sodium and water back into your body. Studies on alcohol and the intestine have shown that alcohol can interfere with the transport systems these cells rely on, and that heavier drinking can temporarily damage the lining itself. Less absorption upstream means more water left in the gut, and the result is looser, more urgent stools.

Alcohol can also reduce the activity of digestive enzymes on the surface of the small intestine. One of them is lactase, the enzyme that digests the sugar in milk. That's why a late-night pizza, a creamy cocktail, or a latte the next morning can hit harder than usual after drinking, even if dairy normally doesn't bother you.

### 3. Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach and bowel

Alcohol is an irritant to the delicate lining of the digestive tract. In the stomach it increases acid and can cause inflammation (gastritis), which is part of why hangovers come with nausea and that burning, unsettled feeling. Further along, irritation of the intestinal lining can trigger the gut to secrete more fluid and contract more, both of which push toward diarrhea.

### 4. Alcohol makes the gut lining leakier and disturbs gut bacteria

Research in this area suggests that alcohol loosens the tight seals between the cells lining your intestines, which scientists describe as increased intestinal permeability, or a "leaky gut." It also shifts the balance of bacteria living in your gut. A single night out is unlikely to cause lasting changes, but these effects can add to short-term digestive upset, and they matter more for people who drink heavily on a regular basis. If you want the longer story, our guide to [how alcohol affects your gut microbiome](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-affects-your-gut-microbiome-the-hidden-health-impact-2025) goes deeper.

### 5. What you drank it with matters as much as the alcohol

A lot of next-day diarrhea isn't really caused by ethanol alone. It's caused by everything that came with it:

- **Sugary mixers and cocktails.** Large amounts of sugar, especially fructose (in juice, soda, and syrups), can draw water into the gut when more arrives than your small intestine can absorb. Some people absorb fructose poorly to begin with.
- **Sugar-free mixers.** Diet mixers and some "low-sugar" seltzers use sugar alcohols or sweeteners that are known to cause loose stools in larger amounts.
- **Carbonation.** Bubbles add gas and bloating and can make cramping worse.
- **Late-night food.** Greasy, fried, and spicy food is a classic trigger. Fat can speed up the colon's contractions after a meal, and capsaicin in spicy food irritates the gut on the way through.
- **Caffeine.** Energy-drink mixers and the morning coffee both stimulate the colon. Coffee on its own is enough to send many people to the bathroom; on top of an irritated gut, it can be the final push.
- **Volume.** Drinking several pints of beer means pouring a lot of fluid and fermentable carbohydrate through your system in a few hours.

## Diarrhea After Drinking Liquor: Is It Different?

People often notice that liquor nights and beer nights feel different the next morning, and they're not imagining it. The core effects on gut speed, absorption, and irritation apply to any alcoholic drink, but there are some real differences.

**Concentration.** Spirits are around 40% alcohol, compared with about 5% for beer and 12 to 14% for wine. Undiluted or lightly mixed liquor reaches the stomach lining at a much higher strength, which is more irritating. Shots on an empty stomach are the worst-case version. Research on stomach emptying suggests stronger drinks also tend to sit in the stomach longer, which can mean nausea first and diarrhea later as everything moves on.

**Mixers.** With liquor, the mixer often does as much damage as the spirit. A night of rum and cola, vodka and energy drinks, or margaritas made with sweet mix delivers a lot of sugar, caffeine, acid, and carbonation alongside the alcohol.

**Congeners.** Darker spirits like whiskey, brandy, and dark rum contain more congeners, which are by-products of fermentation and aging that add flavor. Studies have linked higher-congener drinks to worse hangovers overall. There's no strong evidence tying congeners specifically to diarrhea, but if dark liquor consistently wrecks your stomach, switching to a clear spirit with a low-sugar mixer is a reasonable experiment.

**Pace.** Liquor makes it easy to drink a lot of alcohol quickly. Since the gut effects scale with how much you drink, the same night measured in standard drinks will usually be rougher on liquor simply because you drank more of it, faster.

## Beer, Wine, and Other Specific Triggers

**Beer.** Beer is high volume, carbonated, and contains fermentable carbohydrates from grain, plus yeast residue in unfiltered styles. All of that can lead to gas, bloating, and loose stools. Beer is also made from barley (and sometimes wheat), so it contains gluten unless it's labeled gluten-free. If you have celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity, beer is a common hidden trigger. Our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) covers the other reasons beer hits differently.

**Wine.** Wine is acidic, and some people react to compounds like histamine and sulfites. Reactions vary a lot between people. Sweet and dessert wines also carry more sugar.

**Cocktails.** Creamy drinks (White Russians, eggnog, Irish cream) can cause trouble for anyone with even mild lactose intolerance, especially since alcohol lowers lactase activity. Fruity cocktails pile on fructose.

**Existing gut conditions.** If you have irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), inflammatory bowel disease, or celiac disease, alcohol is a well-known flare trigger. Many people with IBS find that beer and sugary cocktails are worse than a small amount of a clear spirit or dry wine, but this is very individual. If drinking reliably causes significant gut symptoms, it's worth raising with a doctor, because it may be pointing to an underlying condition rather than just a rough night.

## How Long Does Diarrhea After Drinking Last?

For a typical night out, alcohol-related diarrhea usually shows up the next morning and settles within about 24 hours, sometimes stretching into a second day after a heavy session. Your gut lining repairs itself quickly, and once the alcohol and the irritating food are out of your system, things tend to return to normal.

If it's still going after 2 days, that's longer than a typical hangover and worth getting checked. It may be something else entirely, like a stomach bug or food poisoning picked up the same night, a reaction to a medication, or a sign of an underlying condition.

A note on stool color: alcohol and some drinks can change stool color a bit (dark beers, red wine, and blue or green cocktails are common culprits), and bismuth medicines like Pepto-Bismol can turn stool and your tongue black harmlessly. But black, tarry, sticky stool that isn't explained by bismuth, or any visible blood, can be a sign of bleeding in the digestive tract and needs prompt medical attention.

## What to Do: How to Stop Diarrhea After Drinking

There's no instant fix, but the following steps help your body recover and keep you from getting dehydrated, which is the main risk.

### Rehydrate properly, not just with water

Diarrhea loses both water and salts, and alcohol already increases urine output by suppressing a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Plain water helps, but a drink that contains some sodium and a little sugar is absorbed better, because your gut uses sugar to help pull sodium and water in. Good options:

- An oral rehydration solution (the kind sold in pharmacies for diarrhea)
- Broth or clear soup
- An electrolyte drink, ideally one that isn't loaded with sugar
- Diluted fruit juice, if that's what you have

Sip steadily rather than gulping a liter at once, which can set off cramping. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) explains timing, and our roundup of [hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares common options.

### Eat small, bland meals

You don't need to fast. Eating small amounts of easy food helps your gut recover and gives it something to work with. Good choices include toast, crackers, rice, bananas, oatmeal, boiled potatoes, plain chicken, and eggs. For the rest of the day, go easy on fried and fatty food, very spicy food, dairy (especially if it bothered you the night before), and lots of raw vegetables or high-fiber foods.

### Hold off on coffee and more alcohol

Coffee stimulates the colon. If you need caffeine to function, have a smaller cup after you've eaten something. And skip the "hair of the dog." More alcohol only delays recovery and keeps irritating your gut.

### Over-the-counter medicines: use with care

- **Loperamide (Imodium).** Loperamide slows the gut and can help with simple, watery diarrhea. Follow the label dose exactly. Don't use it if you have blood in your stool, black stool, or a fever, because in those cases diarrhea may be your body clearing an infection and slowing it down can make things worse. If you're not sure, ask a pharmacist.
- **Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol).** This can help with an upset stomach and diarrhea, but it contains a salicylate, a relative of aspirin. Its US label carries a stomach bleeding warning for people who have 3 or more alcoholic drinks a day, and it isn't suitable for people who are allergic to aspirin, take blood thinners, or are under 12. It can also turn your stool and tongue black, which is harmless but confusing.
- **Painkillers.** If you also have a headache, be aware that ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already inflamed. Acetaminophen is easier on the stomach but harder on the liver after drinking. Our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains how to use it safely.

If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding anything new, since some medicines interact with alcohol and with each other.

### Rest

Sleep after drinking is lighter and more broken than normal, and your body does a lot of its repair work while you rest. If you can, take it easy for the day.

## How to Prevent Diarrhea After Drinking Next Time

Since the effects of alcohol on the gut scale with how much you drink and how fast, prevention mostly comes down to a few habits:

1. **Eat a real meal before you drink.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches the intestines and blunts the irritation from strong drinks. A meal with some protein, fat, and starch works better than a snack.
2. **Pace yourself.** Roughly one standard drink an hour, with water in between, gives your body a chance to keep up.
3. **Choose your mixers carefully.** Soda water and a squeeze of citrus are gentler than sugary sodas, sweet mixes, or energy drinks. Watch out for sugar-free mixers with sugar alcohols if they tend to bother you.
4. **Know your personal triggers.** If beer always does it, try something else. If creamy cocktails do it, skip them. If you suspect gluten, look for gluten-free options or ask a doctor about testing.
5. **Be careful with late-night food.** Greasy, spicy food after drinking is one of the most reliable diarrhea triggers. Toast or a plain sandwich is less exciting but far kinder.
6. **Drink water before bed.** Going to sleep less dehydrated makes the next morning easier on every front.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence behind them. And if nausea is the bigger problem for you, see our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025).

## When Diarrhea After Drinking Is a Warning Sign

For most people, an occasional bout of loose stools after a big night is just part of the hangover. But a few patterns deserve attention:

- **Diarrhea every time you drink, even a little.** This can point to an underlying issue such as IBS, celiac disease, lactose intolerance, or another digestive condition. It's worth mentioning to a doctor.
- **Ongoing diarrhea in someone who drinks heavily most days.** Long-term heavy drinking can damage the lining of the gut and affect the pancreas, which makes the enzymes you need to digest fat. Pale, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float or are hard to flush can be a sign that fat isn't being absorbed properly. That needs a medical evaluation.
- **Severe upper abdominal pain**, especially if it spreads to your back and comes with vomiting. This can be a sign of pancreatitis, which can be triggered by heavy drinking and needs urgent care.
- **Blood, black tarry stools, fever, or signs of dehydration.** These are not normal hangover symptoms. See a doctor.
- **Symptoms when you cut back.** For people who drink heavily every day, stopping suddenly can trigger alcohol withdrawal. Diarrhea can be part of it, along with tremor, sweating, anxiety, a fast heartbeat, and trouble sleeping. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so don't try to tough it out alone. A doctor can help you cut back safely.

## What About Supplements?

You'll see plenty of hangover products that promise to settle your stomach. Here's an honest view.

For the gut itself, the evidence-backed tools are still the basic ones: oral rehydration, food, time, and drinking less. Some people find probiotics or ginger helpful for general digestive comfort, but there is no good evidence that any supplement prevents alcohol-related diarrhea specifically. If you want to read more about supporting your gut if you drink, our guide to [gut health and alcohol](/never-hungover/gut-health-alcohol-microbiome-protection) covers what the research does and doesn't show.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It isn't a diarrhea remedy, and there is no good evidence that it protects your gut from alcohol. Some people take it as part of their overall routine for nights out, alongside eating, pacing, and hydrating. If you want to try DHM, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when. No supplement replaces drinking less, and none makes heavy drinking safe.

## The Bottom Line

Diarrhea after drinking happens because alcohol speeds up your gut, makes it worse at absorbing water and salt, and irritates its lining, while the sugar, bubbles, caffeine, and greasy food that often come with drinking add to the problem. Liquor can hit harder because it's stronger and usually comes with sweet, fizzy mixers. Rehydrate with something that contains salt, eat small bland meals, skip coffee and more alcohol for the day, and expect it to settle within a day or so. See a doctor if there's blood, black stool, fever, severe pain, dehydration, or if it lasts more than 2 days, and talk to a doctor if it happens every time you drink or if you drink heavily most days.

faq.question: Why do I get diarrhea after drinking alcohol?
faq.answer: Alcohol speeds up the movement of your small intestine, reduces how much water and salt your gut absorbs, and irritates the lining of your stomach and bowel. Sugary mixers, carbonation, caffeine, and greasy late-night food add to the effect. The result is more fluid reaching the colon faster than it can be absorbed, which means loose, urgent stools the next morning.

faq.question: Why does liquor give me diarrhea?
faq.answer: Spirits are much stronger than beer or wine, so they irritate the stomach and gut lining more, especially as shots or on an empty stomach. Liquor is also often mixed with sugary sodas, sweet mixes, or energy drinks, which add sugar, caffeine, and carbonation. And because liquor is easy to drink quickly, people often end up having more alcohol overall.

faq.question: How long does diarrhea after drinking last?
faq.answer: Usually less than 24 hours, sometimes into a second day after a heavy night. If it lasts more than 2 days, or comes with blood, black stools, fever, severe pain, or signs of dehydration, see a doctor, because it may be something other than a hangover.

faq.question: How do I stop diarrhea after drinking?
faq.answer: Rehydrate with fluids that contain some salt and sugar, such as an oral rehydration solution or broth, eat small bland meals like toast, rice, and bananas, and avoid coffee, more alcohol, and greasy or spicy food for the day. Loperamide (Imodium) at the label dose can help with simple watery diarrhea, but don't use it if you have blood in your stool, black stool, or a fever.

faq.question: Can I take Imodium or Pepto-Bismol after drinking?
faq.answer: Loperamide (Imodium) is generally fine for simple watery diarrhea if you follow the label dose and don't have blood in your stool, black stool, or a fever. Pepto-Bismol contains a salicylate, a relative of aspirin, and its label warns about stomach bleeding for people who have 3 or more drinks a day. Ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines or aren't sure.

faq.question: Is diarrhea after drinking a sign of liver damage?
faq.answer: Not usually. Occasional diarrhea after a night out is a normal hangover symptom caused by the effects of alcohol on the gut. But ongoing diarrhea, pale or greasy stools, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or severe upper belly pain in someone who drinks heavily can signal problems with the liver or pancreas and should be checked by a doctor.

faq.question: Why does beer give me diarrhea more than other drinks?
faq.answer: Beer means drinking a large volume of carbonated fluid that contains fermentable carbohydrates from grain, which can cause gas, bloating, and loose stools. It also contains gluten unless labeled gluten-free, so it can be a trigger for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

faq.question: Does DHM help with diarrhea after drinking?
faq.answer: There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats alcohol-related diarrhea. Its research focuses on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animal studies. For the gut, the tools that help are eating before drinking, pacing, choosing gentler mixers, rehydrating with electrolytes, and drinking less.
